title: No blame today
hookLine: entering Mecca, the Prophet echoes Joseph: no blame on you today (Quran 12:92)

lines: THE CITY THAT DROVE HIM OUT.
cards: What do you say to the people who pushed you out of your home, on the day you walk back in and could do anything you like to them? The early biographies say the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, faced exactly that.

Years after leaving Mecca, he returned with a large following, and the city opened to him. The men who had mocked him, fought him and driven his followers away were gathered, waiting to hear what would happen to them.
Tradition says he didn't make up a new answer. He borrowed one from an older story.

teach.b: The older story is in the Qur'an's surah of Joseph. His brothers throw him into a well, and he is sold away. Much later he is a powerful man in Egypt, and the brothers come before him needing grain, not knowing who he is.
When at last he tells them, they admit they were in the wrong. His answer comes at chapter twelve, verse ninety-two.

teach.h: NO BLAME ON YOU THIS DAY.
teach.b: In paraphrase: there is no blame on you this day; may God forgive you, and he is the most merciful of those who show mercy. No speech about the well. No list of what it cost him.
The case is closed in a sentence, and the rest is handed to God. Now the echo.
In the sira, when Mecca opened to him, the Prophet asked the Quraysh, his own tribe, what they expected from him. In the telling, they answered that they expected good from a generous brother.
And he answered with Joseph's words. Tradition adds that he told them to go; they were free.

teach.h: A CASE CLOSED ON A NAMED DAY.
teach.b: A grudge is a case kept open, filed and ready to be pulled out.
No blame today closes it, on a day you can name. It doesn't say nothing happened; Joseph's brothers knew exactly what happened, and said so.
It says the account won't be pressed, and it comes from someone who had every means to press it.

how: Muslims read Joseph's words in surah 12 and tell the sira's account of the Prophet repeating them at Mecca; the phrase is quoted when people are urged to forgive old enemies.

the people of Medina who welcomed the Prophet

games.q: no blame today — tap the pairs.
p: thrown in a well, later in power
no blame on you this day
where the Mecca telling comes from

s: Joseph lists every wrong before he forgives his brothers
in the Qur'an's telling he closes it in a sentence: no blame on you this day.
the Qur'an itself describes the Prophet's words at Mecca
the Qur'an gives Joseph's words; the scene at Mecca comes from the sira.
Joseph adds that God may forgive them
same verse: may God forgive you, the most merciful of those who show mercy.

games.q: you're Joseph. the brothers who threw you in a well stand before you and admit they were wrong. what do you say?
o: first, let me tell you what it cost me.
no blame on you this day.
earn it back, and then we'll see.
games.why: he closes it in a sentence and hands the rest to God. the sira says the Prophet borrowed the same words at Mecca.

practice: Bring up one grudge you've kept open, not the biggest, and picture it as a file on a desk, the evidence all in order.
Without arguing the case again, close the cover and quietly name today: not that it didn't happen, only that from today the account isn't pressed.
If you pray, you can hand the rest to God in your own tradition's words; if you don't, set the file down and leave it there.

wordCard.voice: Quraysh. The Prophet's own tribe, asked what they expected from him when Mecca opened to him, and answered with Joseph's words. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, Qur'an 12:92: no blame on you this day.

carryVoice: Your line: the account won't be pressed. If it comes knocking tomorrow, the date still stands. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

sources.work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq, in Ibn Hisham's recension)
